questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of the world's population lives in Asia?
options: About 30%
About 80%
About 15%
About 60%
questions.explanation: Asia holds roughly six in every ten of the world's people, with China and India alone accounting for over a third of the total. Thirty per cent would be closer to the combined share of Africa and Europe.

questions.stem: Which of these regions is sparsely populated?
options: The interior of the Sahara
The Nile valley and delta in Egypt
The plain of the Ganges River in India
The island of Java in Indonesia
questions.explanation: Hot deserts lack reliable water and fertile soil, so they support few people. The Nile valley, the Ganges plain and Java are among the most densely populated regions on Earth.

questions.stem: Egypt's Nile valley is densely populated, while desert a few kilometres either side is almost empty. This shows a strong spatial association between population density and:
options: the distance from the country's coastline
the latitude of each part of the country
the height of the land above sea level
a reliable water supply and fertile soils
questions.explanation: The ribbon of dense settlement follows the river's water and fertile floodplain soils almost exactly, so the two distributions match closely. Latitude and altitude barely change across the valley and the nearby desert, so they cannot explain the contrast.

questions.stem: The crude birth rate is the number of:
options: children born to each woman over her lifetime
live births per 1000 women aged 15 to 49 in a year
babies who survive to one year per 1000 live births
live births per 1000 people in a year
questions.explanation: The crude birth rate relates births to the whole population. The average number of children per woman is the total fertility rate, a different measure.

questions.stem: The infant mortality rate is the number of:
options: deaths of mothers during childbirth per 100 000 live births in a year
deaths of all people per 1000 of the population in a year
deaths of children under one year of age per 1000 live births in a year
deaths of children under five years of age per 1000 people in the population
questions.explanation: Infant mortality counts deaths before the first birthday against the number of live births. Deaths of all people per 1000 is the crude death rate.

questions.stem: The total fertility rate is:
options: the percentage of women of child-bearing age who give birth to a live baby in a given year
the number of live births minus the number of deaths per 1000 people in a year
the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime at current rates
the number of live births per 1000 people in the whole population in a year
questions.explanation: The total fertility rate is expressed as children per woman, such as 1.6 or 5.2. Births per 1000 people is the crude birth rate, and births minus deaths gives natural increase.

questions.stem: Replacement-level fertility in low-mortality countries is about 2.1 children per woman rather than 2.0 because:
options: each couple must replace themselves and also one grandparent in the population
immigration adds about 0.1 children per woman to most countries' populations
women who have no children are counted as having 0.1 children in the data
some children die before adulthood and slightly more boys than girls are born
questions.explanation: To replace two parents, each woman needs on average just over one daughter who survives to child-bearing age; child deaths and a sex ratio at birth of about 105 boys per 100 girls lift the figure to about 2.1. Immigration is not part of the fertility rate.

questions.stem: The world region with the highest average total fertility rate is:
options: East Asia
Europe
Latin America and the Caribbean
sub-Saharan Africa
questions.explanation: Fertility in sub-Saharan Africa remains well above that of any other world region. East Asia and Europe have fertility well below replacement level.

questions.stem: Why is high infant mortality often spatially associated with high fertility?
options: High fertility causes infant deaths directly, because large families have more births
Infant deaths are counted as births in the data, so fertility appears higher than it is
Areas with high infant mortality always have the most doctors per person in the country
Parents may have more children so that some survive, and both reflect limited health care
questions.explanation: Where many infants die, families tend to have more children to ensure some reach adulthood, and both patterns are linked to poor access to health care, education and family planning. The two are measured separately, so one does not inflate the other in the data.

questions.stem: A country's crude birth rate is 32 per 1000 and its crude death rate is 8 per 1000. Ignoring migration, its rate of natural increase is:
options: 4.0% per year
2.4% per year
24% per year
0.24% per year
questions.explanation: Natural increase is 32 − 8 = 24 per 1000, and 24 per 1000 is 2.4 per 100, or 2.4%. Reading 24 per 1000 as 24% confuses a rate per thousand with a percentage.

questions.stem: A hypothetical country has a crude birth rate of 30 per 1000 and a crude death rate of 16 per 1000. Using the rule of 70 and ignoring migration, its population would double in about:
options: 5 years
50 years
23 years
15 years
questions.explanation: Natural increase is 30 − 16 = 14 per 1000, or 1.4% a year, and 70 ÷ 1.4 = 50 years. Using the birth rate alone gives 70 ÷ 3.0 ≈ 23 years.

questions.stem: In one year a hypothetical country records 300 000 births, 200 000 deaths, 150 000 immigrants and 50 000 emigrants. By how much did its population change?
options: An increase of 250 000
An increase of 700 000
An increase of 200 000
An increase of 100 000
questions.explanation: Natural increase is 300 000 − 200 000 = 100 000 and net migration is 150 000 − 50 000 = 100 000, so the population grew by 200 000. The figure of 100 000 counts natural increase only and leaves out migration.

questions.stem: World population first reached about one billion around:
questions.explanation: World population reached one billion in the early 1800s after thousands of years of slow growth. By 1950 it had reached about 2.5 billion.

questions.stem: The annual growth rate of world population reached its peak in the:
options: 2010s, at about 3% a year
1960s, at just over 2% a year
1800s, at about 5% a year during industrialisation
1920s, at about 1% a year
questions.explanation: Growth peaked at a little over 2% a year in the 1960s and has fallen since, to around half that rate. A rate of 5% a year has never been reached for the world as a whole.

questions.stem: A student reads that the growth rate of world population has roughly halved since the 1960s and concludes that world population must now be shrinking. Why is this wrong?
options: Growth rates measure births only, so they cannot tell us anything about whether a population is shrinking
World population cannot shrink, because death rates are now lower than at any time in the past
A smaller positive growth rate still adds people each year; a population shrinks only if the rate is negative
The growth rate has actually doubled since the 1960s, so world population is growing faster than ever
questions.explanation: A lower but positive rate means slower growth, not decline, and because it applies to a much larger population the number added each year has stayed high. Populations can shrink, but only when deaths and emigration exceed births and immigration.

questions.stem: Most projections suggest that during the 21st century world population will:
options: begin falling immediately and halve by the end of the century
remain exactly at its present size for the rest of the century
keep growing at a slowing rate, possibly reaching a peak later in the century
grow at an accelerating rate, doubling roughly every 35 years until 2100
questions.explanation: Falling fertility in most regions means growth is slowing, and projections show world population levelling off or peaking later this century. The timing and size of the peak differ between projections, but none show accelerating growth.

questions.stem: The rapid growth of world population after 1950 was mainly the result of:
options: death rates falling sharply in developing countries while birth rates stayed high
birth rates rising sharply in developed countries after the end of the Second World War
large-scale migration from developed countries to developing countries after 1950
life expectancy falling in most countries as a result of rapid urbanisation
questions.explanation: Vaccination, antibiotics, clean water and better food supplies cut death rates quickly in developing countries, while birth rates fell more slowly, so natural increase rose. Post-war baby booms in developed countries were real but involved a much smaller share of the world's people.

questions.stem: Which development helps explain why life expectancy fell in several southern African countries during the 1990s and early 2000s?
options: Falling fertility rates
Rising rates of literacy
The spread of HIV/AIDS
The Green Revolution
questions.explanation: HIV/AIDS caused high death rates among young and middle-aged adults in countries such as Botswana and Zimbabwe, lowering life expectancy until treatment became widely available. The Green Revolution and rising literacy tend to raise life expectancy rather than lower it.

questions.stem: A population pyramid shows a population's:
options: rate of growth in each year over a long period
movements between regions over a whole decade
structure by age group and sex at a point in time
density in each region of the country in one year
questions.explanation: A pyramid uses horizontal bars for each age group, males on one side and females on the other, to show the structure at one date. Comparing pyramids from different dates shows change over time.

questions.stem: A population pyramid with a wide base that narrows steeply towards the top indicates:
options: a low birth rate and an ageing population with relatively high life expectancy
a birth rate below the death rate, so that the population is now steadily declining
a large inflow of working-age immigrants on temporary labour contracts
a high birth rate and a youthful population with relatively low life expectancy
questions.explanation: A wide base means many births, and the steep narrowing shows that relatively few people survive to old age. An ageing population with low fertility has a narrow base, giving a constrictive shape.

questions.stem: A population pyramid whose base is narrower than the bars for people aged 30 to 50 most likely shows:
options: a rise in the birth rate over recent decades
a rise in infant mortality in recent decades
the emigration of most people aged 30 to 50
a fall in the birth rate over recent decades
questions.explanation: Fewer children than adults means fewer births in recent years than a generation ago, giving a constrictive pyramid. Emigration of people aged 30 to 50 would narrow those bars, not widen them relative to the base.

questions.stem: A pyramid shows about three times as many males as females aged 20 to 49, but similar numbers of boys and girls under 15. The most likely cause is:
options: a policy limiting births that led families to favour sons
much higher female life expectancy among the working-age group
large-scale immigration of male workers on temporary contracts
a long war that killed many young women in the population
questions.explanation: An imbalance that appears only in working ages, while children are evenly balanced, points to migrant labour, as in some Gulf states. A preference for sons would distort the sex ratio from birth, including among children, and never by a factor of three.

questions.stem: In a hypothetical country, 30% of people are aged 0–14, 60% are aged 15–64 and 10% are aged 65 and over. Its dependency ratio is about:
options: 17 dependants per 100 people of working age
67 dependants per 100 people of working age
40 dependants per 100 people of working age
150 dependants per 100 people of working age
questions.explanation: The dependency ratio is (0–14 plus 65 and over) ÷ 15–64 × 100, so (30 + 10) ÷ 60 × 100 ≈ 67. The figure of 40 is the share of dependants in the total population, not per 100 people of working age.

questions.stem: A hypothetical country's pyramid shows a large bulge at ages 60 to 74 and a smaller bulge at ages 30 to 44. The smaller bulge is best explained as:
options: a fall in the birth rate during the years they were born
the children of the large generation now aged 60 to 74
a rise in deaths among people aged 30 to 44 in recent years
the emigration of people aged 30 to 44 to other countries
questions.explanation: A large baby-boom generation produces many births when its members are in their child-bearing years, creating an 'echo' about 30 years younger. More deaths, emigration or fewer births would make those bars smaller, not form a bulge.

questions.stem: Stage 1 of the Demographic Transition Model is characterised by:
options: falling birth rates and low death rates, with slowing growth
birth rates below death rates, with the population declining
high birth rates and high, fluctuating death rates, with little growth
high birth rates and rapidly falling death rates, with very rapid growth
questions.explanation: In stage 1, high death rates from disease, famine and war offset high birth rates, so population grows little. Rapidly falling death rates with high birth rates describe stage 2.

questions.stem: In stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model, population grows rapidly because:
options: death rates rise because more people live in crowded and polluted cities
large numbers of immigrants arrive from countries in the later stages of the model
death rates fall with better food, water and health care, while birth rates stay high
birth rates rise sharply as families decide to have more children than before
questions.explanation: Improvements in food supply, sanitation and medicine lower death rates quickly, but birth rates remain high for some time, so the gap between them widens. The model does not include migration.

questions.stem: Which change most directly marks a country's move from stage 2 to stage 3 of the Demographic Transition Model?
options: The death rate begins to fall significantly
The birth rate rises above the death rate
The death rate rises above the birth rate
The birth rate begins to fall significantly
questions.explanation: Stage 3 begins when birth rates start to fall, through access to contraception, women's education and work, urbanisation and lower infant mortality. The fall in death rates is what begins stage 2.

questions.stem: A hypothetical country's crude birth rate has stayed at about 44 per 1000 for decades, while its crude death rate has fallen from 30 to 12 per 1000. It is in stage:
options: 2 of the Demographic Transition Model
1 of the Demographic Transition Model
4 of the Demographic Transition Model
5 of the Demographic Transition Model
questions.explanation: A high, steady birth rate with a sharply falling death rate is the pattern of stage 2, with rapid natural increase. In stage 1 the death rate would still be high and close to the birth rate.

questions.stem: A hypothetical country has a crude birth rate of 13, a crude death rate of 9 and a total fertility rate of 1.6. Which stage of the Demographic Transition Model best fits these data?
options: Stage 3, because the birth rate is still well above the death rate and rising
Stage 4, because birth and death rates are both low and births still exceed deaths
Stage 5, because fertility is below replacement level, so the population must be falling
Stage 1, because the rate of natural increase is low, as it is before any transition
questions.explanation: Both rates are low and births still exceed deaths, giving slow natural increase, which fits stage 4. Fertility below replacement will lead to decline in time, but stage 5 requires the birth rate to fall below the death rate, which has not yet happened.

questions.stem: In stage 5 of the Demographic Transition Model:
options: the birth rate falls below the death rate and the population ages and declines
the death rate falls below the birth rate and the population grows rapidly
both rates rise together and the population structure becomes more youthful
both rates are high and the population structure has a very wide, expansive base
questions.explanation: Stage 5 describes natural decrease, with very low fertility and an old population structure. Rapid growth from a falling death rate is stage 2.

questions.stem: A wealthy country's crude death rate rose from 7 to 10 per 1000 over 30 years, while life expectancy also rose. The best explanation is that:
options: health care declined over the period, so people of every age were more likely to die each year
life expectancy is calculated from the birth rate, so it can rise even when health care is poor
more babies were born over the period, and infants have the highest death rates of any age group
the population aged, so a larger share of people were in old age groups where deaths are more frequent
questions.explanation: The crude death rate depends on age structure: an older population has more deaths per 1000 even when each age group is healthier than before. Rising life expectancy shows that health was improving, not declining.

questions.stem: A limitation of the Demographic Transition Model is that it:
options: predicts that every country will remain in stage 1 for the rest of its history
does not include migration, which can be the main source of change for some countries
applies only to the number of migrants and cannot be used with birth or death rates
was designed for developing countries, so it does not fit the countries of Western Europe
questions.explanation: The model shows only natural change, yet migration drives population change in countries such as Australia and the Gulf states. It was based on the historical experience of Western Europe, which is why its fit to developing countries is questioned.

questions.stem: Thomas Malthus argued that, if unchecked, population tends to grow:
options: at the same rate as food supply, so that famine can never occur in any country
only when food supply falls, because hunger encourages families to have more children
geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8) while food supply grows arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4)
arithmetically (1, 2, 3, 4) while food supply grows geometrically (1, 2, 4, 8)
questions.explanation: Malthus's 1798 essay argued that population would outstrip food supply, because doubling growth eventually overtakes steady additions. Reversing the two growth patterns is the most common error.

questions.stem: Under Malthusian theory, delaying marriage and having fewer children is an example of:
options: a positive check, which lowers the birth rate
a preventive check, which lowers the birth rate
a positive check, which raises the death rate
a preventive check, which raises the death rate
questions.explanation: Malthus described preventive checks, such as moral restraint and later marriage, which reduce births, and positive checks, such as famine, disease and war, which increase deaths. 'Positive' here does not mean desirable.

questions.stem: Which development is most often cited as evidence against Malthus's predictions?
options: The rapid growth of world population after 1950, which matched his forecast of geometric growth
The Green Revolution, which raised crop yields faster than population grew in many countries
The famines of the 20th century, which showed that population outstripped food in some places
The rise in death rates in stage 1 countries, which showed that positive checks were operating
questions.explanation: High-yielding crop varieties, irrigation and fertilisers allowed food production to keep ahead of population in much of Asia and Latin America. Famines and rapid population growth are usually used to support Malthus, not challenge him.

questions.stem: Which argument best supports the continuing relevance of Malthusian theory to sustainability?
options: Technology has removed all environmental limits on food production for the future
Growing population and consumption may exceed what land, water and ecosystems can sustain
World food production has always risen faster than population, so shortages cannot occur
Population growth has stopped in every country, so the theory no longer applies anywhere in the world
questions.explanation: Neo-Malthusians apply his idea of limits to modern pressures such as water scarcity, soil degradation and climate change, linking population to environmental sustainability. Claims that limits have vanished or that growth has stopped everywhere are false.

questions.stem: Ester Boserup's view contrasts with Malthus's because she argued that:
options: food supply grows geometrically while population grows only arithmetically over time
famine is the only check that can bring population back into balance with food supply
populations should be reduced by law to the number that traditional farming can support
population pressure stimulates farmers to adopt new techniques that increase food output
questions.explanation: Boserup saw a growing population as a driver of agricultural intensification, so food supply responds to population rather than limiting it. The other views either restate Malthusian checks or reverse his growth patterns.

questions.stem: Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, a refugee is a person who:
options: has been forced from their home but remains within their own country
has moved to another country for a period of study at a foreign university
is outside their country because of a well-founded fear of persecution
has left their country voluntarily to find better-paid work elsewhere
questions.explanation: The Convention covers persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, and requires the person to be outside their country. People displaced within their own country are internally displaced persons.

questions.stem: Families flee severe flooding to a city in another province of their own country. This movement is best classified as:
options: voluntary and internal
forced and external
voluntary and external
forced and internal
questions.explanation: A hazard event drove the movement, so it is forced, and it did not cross an international border, so it is internal. Moving to another province is still within the same country.

questions.stem: Workers from a Pacific Island country travel to Victoria each year to pick fruit for six months, then return home. Their movement is best classified as:
options: forced, external and short term
voluntary, external and short term
forced, internal and long term (permanent)
voluntary, internal and long term
questions.explanation: The workers choose to go, cross an international border and return each year, so the movement is voluntary, external and short term (circular). It would be internal only if they stayed within their own country.

questions.stem: China's hukou (household registration) system has affected internal migration because it:
options: prevents anyone born in a city from moving to a rural area at any stage of their life
pays rural migrants a bonus for each year they live and work in one of the coastal cities
ties access to services such as schooling and health care to a person's registered home
requires every rural family to send one member to work in a city for at least ten years
questions.explanation: Many rural-to-urban migrants remain registered in their home villages, so they have had limited access to urban services, and many children were left behind with grandparents. The system restricts entitlements; it does not compel migration.

questions.stem: A rural region's pyramid shows a deficit of people aged 20 to 39 and a large share aged over 65, while the national pyramid does not. The most likely explanation is that:
options: the region has received large numbers of young immigrants from overseas in recent years
young adults have migrated from the region to cities for work and education
the region's birth rate has been much higher than the national birth rate
older people have been leaving the region to retire in the nation's cities
questions.explanation: Out-migration of young adults removes people from the working ages and leaves an older population behind, so movement changes the region's structure. Older people leaving would shrink, not enlarge, the over-65 share.

questions.stem: Two hypothetical states in one country: State P has female literacy of 95%, infant mortality of 7 and a fertility rate of 1.8; State Q has 55%, 45 and 3.4. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Fertility cannot differ within a country, because the same national policies apply everywhere
Higher female literacy causes higher infant mortality, as State Q's figures clearly demonstrate
State Q has lower fertility than State P, because its infant mortality rate is much higher
Within one country, lower fertility is spatially associated with female education and child survival
questions.explanation: State P combines high female literacy, low infant mortality and low fertility, while State Q shows the reverse, so the variables are associated across space. Association alone does not prove which factor causes which, but the pattern is clear.

questions.stem: Which feature of China's population structure is most directly linked to the one-child policy?
options: A large surplus of women in the working-age groups
A sharp rise in the birth rate from the early 1980s
A narrowing base after 1980 and more boys than girls born each year
A wide, expanding base among children born after 1980
questions.explanation: Limiting most families to one child narrowed the base of the pyramid, and a preference for sons skewed the sex ratio at birth towards boys. The policy reduced births, so it could not widen the base or raise the birth rate.
